questions.question_text: What is the gradient of the line $y = 6x - 5$?

options.why: Read the constant term $c$ as the gradient instead of the coefficient of $x$.
Took the constant without its sign; that value is the $y$-intercept, not the gradient.
Reversed the sign of the coefficient of $x$, which is already positive.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is the coefficient of $x$.
$m = 6$

questions.question_text: What is the gradient of the line $y = -4x + 7$?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the coefficient of $x$.
Read the constant term as the gradient instead of the coefficient of $x$.
Read the constant and changed its sign; the gradient is the coefficient of $x$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is the coefficient of $x$, including its sign.
$m = -4$

questions.question_text: What is the gradient of the line $y = \frac{3}{5}x + 2$?

options.why: Inverted the fraction; the gradient is the coefficient exactly as written.
Read the constant term as the gradient instead of the coefficient of $x$.
Used only the numerator; the whole fraction is the coefficient of $x$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is the coefficient of $x$.
$m = \frac{3}{5}$

questions.question_text: What are the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the line $y = 2x + 9$?

options.why: Used the gradient as the $y$-intercept instead of the constant term.
Placed the value on the $x$-axis; the $y$-intercept always has $x = 0$.
Reversed the sign of the constant term, which is positive here.

questions.solution_text:
The $y$-intercept is the constant term, written as $(0, c)$.
$(0, 9)$

questions.question_text: What are the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the line $y = 8x - 9$?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the constant term.
Used the gradient as the $y$-intercept instead of the constant.
Placed the value on the $x$-axis; the $y$-intercept always has $x = 0$.

questions.solution_text:
The $y$-intercept is the constant term, written as $(0, c)$.
$(0, -9)$

questions.question_text: What are the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the line $y = 4x$?

options.why: Used the gradient as the $y$-intercept; there is no constant term here.
Placed the gradient on the $x$-axis; a missing constant means the origin.
Assumed a constant of $1$; a missing constant means $c = 0$.

questions.solution_text:
There is no constant term, so $c = 0$.
$(0, 0)$

questions.question_text: What is the gradient of the line $y = 8 - 3x$?

options.why: Read the first number as the gradient; rewrite as $y = -3x + 8$ first.
Dropped the negative sign after rewriting as $y = -3x + 8$.
Took the constant with a sign change instead of the coefficient of $x$.

questions.solution_text:
Rewrite in the order $y = mx + c$.
$y = -3x + 8$
$m = -3$

questions.question_text: Is the line $y = -2x + 11$ increasing or decreasing?

options.why: Ignored the negative gradient; a negative $m$ makes the line fall.
A flat line needs $m = 0$, but here the gradient is $-2$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is $m = -2$.
A negative gradient means the line decreases.
Decreasing.

questions.question_text: Which line is steeper, $y = x + 2$ or $y = 4x + 2$?

options.why: Chose the line with the smaller gradient; steeper means larger gradient size.
Compared the equal $y$-intercepts instead of the gradients.

questions.solution_text:
Steeper lines have a gradient with larger size.
For $y = x + 2$, $m = 1$; for $y = 4x + 2$, $m = 4$.
$4 > 1$, so $y = 4x + 2$ is steeper.

questions.question_text: State the gradient and the $y$-intercept of the line $y = -x + 5$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the hidden coefficient of $x$.
Swapped the gradient and the $y$-intercept value.
Swapped the two values and changed the intercept sign.

questions.solution_text:
The coefficient of $x$ is $-1$.
$m = -1$, and the $y$-intercept is $(0, 5)$.
